what: Cousins Properties owns modern office towers in fast-growing Sun Belt cities - Atlanta, Austin, Charlotte, Tampa, Phoenix, Nashville and Dallas. It develops and leases top-quality buildings to companies relocating or expanding in those markets.
customers: Large corporate tenants in technology, finance, professional services and healthcare, often companies moving operations from high-cost coastal cities.
money: Rent and recoveries from Class A office buildings in Sun Belt markets.
Parking, fees and residential or retail space within its developments.
moat: A portfolio concentrated in the newest, best-located buildings in cities gaining population and employers, the segment of the office market still attracting tenants.
risks: Office demand remains weaker than before the pandemic as companies use less space per worker.
Sun Belt cities have seen new office supply, which can pressure rents.
High interest rates raise financing costs on $3.4 billion of debt and depress office property values.
opportunities: The flight to quality favours the newest buildings, where Cousins is concentrated.
Little new office construction is starting, which should tighten the best part of the market over time.
watch: Leasing volume and occupancy in its key markets. They show whether the flight to quality is translating into rent growth.
view: The P/E of about 319 on Cousins is meaningless, and so is the price to free cash flow of 263: an office REIT’s net income is crushed by depreciation, and its cash flow after development spending swings with construction. The figure that matters is funds from operations per share, and the question is whether the newest Sun Belt office space can keep its occupancy while the wider office market works through a structural decline in demand.

Cousins is the cleanest way to own the thesis that the office market has split in two. Older buildings in coastal downtowns are emptying; new, well-located buildings in growing cities are not. Revenue rising from $755 million in 2021 to $994 million last year, partly through acquisitions, suggests the top end of the market is still functioning. The company has been willing to buy buildings from distressed sellers, which is the right move if the thesis holds.

The market, at $28.71 with analyst targets about 16% higher, is cautious, and caution is appropriate for any office landlord. I think Cousins is among the better-positioned names in a sector that remains out of favour, but this is still a bet on the office cycle turning. Owners need to be patient and comfortable that the best buildings will keep winning tenants as companies tighten their space.
bull: The flight to quality fills its towers, new supply dries up, and rents in the best Sun Belt buildings rise while the sector re-rates.
bear: Hybrid work keeps cutting space demand even in new buildings, Sun Belt supply weighs on rents, and refinancing at higher rates erodes cash flow.
